speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I ask leave, seconded by the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis), in accordance with Standing Order 26, to move the adjournment of the house under the said Standing Order for the purpose of discussing a specific and important matter requiring urgent consideration, namely steps to be 29180-401}
taken by the government of Canada in the light of the continuation of the war in Ni-geria-Biafra and the continued threats of mass starvation and the indiscriminate bombing of civilian targets such as hospitals and market places.
This matter was considered by the house on November 26 last. Since that date the situation has changed, first, by reason of well authenticated reports of frequent instances of bombing of civilians in market places and hospitals far removed from military targets, causing immense loss of life; second, the new initiatives taken by the President of the United States in the appointment of a special coordinator on relief to Nigerian and Biafran war victims and the action of the American government in making stratosphere transport planes available to both the International Red Cross and the church operations; third, the offer of Colonel Ojukwu to construct, with needed outside assistance, an airstrip within Biafran occupied territory to be used exclusively for daylight mercy flights; fourth, the continued Biafran resistance and the prospect of prolongation of the war in the absence of international action, with an increasing toll of lives from starvation.
[DOT] (11:10 a.m.)
In view of these facts urgent consideration by the house is required in order that the government may be directed by parliament to deal effectively with this tragic and urgent humanitarian challenge, which affects the conscience of Canada and the world.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under Standing Order 26 I beg leave, seconded by the hon. member for Egmont (Mr. MacDonald) to move the adjournment of the house for the purpose of discussing a specific and important matter requiring urgent consideration, namely the repudiation by the government of Canada of its commitment to build a solid crossing between Prince Edward Island and the province of New Brunswick.
In any federal state it is essential that undertakings given by one government to another be honoured and respected. The repudiation and disavowal of the commitment by the government of Canada to the people and province of Prince Edward Island in reference to interprovincial transportation, a matter falling within the responsibility of the government of Canada, constitutes a serious diminution of the faith and confidence which is the sine qua non of a viable federal state. The subject he proposes for the consideration of the house under Standing Order 26 is what he terms "a serious diminution of the faith and confidence" essential to a federal state. In this way it seems to me that the hon. member's motion is so general in nature that it can hardly qualify under the terms of the standing order. There are other methods by which executive decisions may be called into question or criticized. speechtext:
The house resumed from Monday, February 24, consideration of the motion of Hon. E. J. Benson (Minister of Finance) that Bill No.
March 7. 1969

C-138, to amend the Bretton Woods Agreement Act and the Currency, Mint and Exchange Fund Act be read the third time and passed.
Hon. Robert L. Staniield (Leader of the
Opposition): Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a few remarks on this bill at this stage. It is concerned with the matter of increasing drawing rights. As previously explained in the house, it is concerned with the matter of providing working capital to countries in connection with expanding world trade. By virtue of the extent of the drawing rights created it may be of some assistance, and no doubt will be of some assistance in providing more time to avert crises and to correct situations where disequilibrium exists; but primarily it is a matter of providing the world with the means of handling expanding world trade.
[DOT] (12 noon)
There has been some discussion in the house concerning whether more measures are required, whether this bill, for example, together with other provisions being made, is adequate to avert the kind of recurring crises we have had in terms of international currencies. I believe I am correct in saying the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) has stated that the government of Canada is giving no consideration to reverting to a floating exchange rate. We recently had a speech by the Governor of the Bank of Canada in which he emphasized the importance of countries pursuing appropriate domestic policies. The Governor has given his view that no possible reforms in international currency arrangements would be able to offset weak or misdirected domestic policies. I wish to state, Mr. Speaker that I discuss any statement made by the Governor of the Bank of Canada with great respect to him. I admire very much the contribution he is making in his office.
I think it is perfectly correct to say, as the Governor of the Bank of Canada said, that no reform of international currency arrangements can possibly be devised which would offset weak or misdirected domestic policies. I believe this is true, but I believe also that it is only part of the story today. This is what I want to emphasize. It is true we could not possibly devise any system of international currency arrangements which would offset or neutralize misdirected domestic policies. Nevertheless, where there is a seriously undervalued or seriously overvalued currency this substantial undervaluation or overvaluation
Finance
does constitute a continuing source of trouble and danger to other countries.
For example, if it is true, as has been suggested, that the German mark is substantially undervalued, this does provide a competitive advantage to West Germany. It also constitutes a constant threat of crisis as a result of continuing speculation that sooner or later there will be some change made in the value of the German mark, that is, that it will be valued upwards or that other currencies will be devalued downwards. As long as this kind of situation exists it constitutes a potential source of crisis. On the other hand, when a situation exists in which a currency is substantially overvalued, as apparently was the case in Britain before the pound was de< al-ued and is now sometimes asserted to be toe case with regard to the French franc, this again constitutes a potential source of crisis.
We can never know when a loss of confidence will suddenly develop with regard to the continuation of affairs as they now exist. Once such a loss of confidence sets in a crisis develops, and it is very difficult to know what countries may be caught up in the crisis. Wt in Canada ought to be very much aware of this after our experience last winter which in turn, of course, followed the devaluation of the pound and the resulting feeling of uncertainty that arose from the devaluation of the pound. No country should have a better understanding than Canada of the rapidity with which crises can develop and the significance that crises can have for our country. Therefore I think we must recognize that where there is in fact either a substantial overvaluation or undervaluation of an important currency this constitutes a source of danger to us.
With all respect to the views expressed by the Governor of the Bank of Canada, I submit it is necessary to provide better machinery than we now have for correcting these situations and for revaluing currencies when they are substantially out of line with reality. Certainly we need arrangements for policing; we need arrangements for encouraging countries to follow appropriate domestic policies. Certainly I agree, as I said before, that no arrangements we make could possibly offset the detrimental effect of misdirected domestic policies. Where a serious disequilibrium develops, however, I suggest we must regard that as a potential source of crisis and danger to other countries including ourselves. We must be interested in developing more satisfactory arrangements for correcting these

March 7, 1969
Finance
overvaluations or undervaluations, as the case may be.
I realize that a good deal of progress has been made with regard to international currency arrangements. We have this bill now before us which represents a very substantial step forward. I would not question that at all. I believe that recently agreements have been reached between the governors of the important central banks in the world with regard to control over the movement of hot or speculative money. These are important steps forward, but I submit in all seriousness that the machinery we have now still remains inadequate and that our own monetary stability can be threatened any time by developments abroad in virtually any part of the developing world. There is a need for an orderly readjustment where necessary rather than just a policy of letting nature take its course because finally we would be confronted by very disorderly readjustments postponed to the point where they are virtual explosions when they take place.
This very day when we are discussing this matter fears exist with regard to uncertainties relating to currencies, which again remind us of how these crises can blow up quickly, of the experience we had last winter, and that it is not good enough, I suggest, simply to put the emphasis upon the importance of countries following appropriate domestic arrangements. Certainly we must emphasize that, but it is in the interests of Canada to seek improved international arrangements for removing serious disequilibriums where they exist.
I say with all respect and I hope all humility that undervaluations and overvaluations can exist which domestic policies will perhaps not correct because they have gone beyond the point where domestic policies can effect the necessary corrections. We must recognize that efforts to correct overvaluations or undervaluations of currencies may result in the development of very severe restrictions on and interference with the flow of international trade. So we need machinery to improve the methods of readjustment. As Canadians we cannot feel easy with matters as they are now. We cannot feel that arrangements today are adequate because we cannot know when we in Canada or indeed the people in virtually any country may suddenly be confronted with a crisis that has developed as a result of a lack of machinery for orderly readjustment.

[DOT] (12:10 p.m.)
No country has a greater interest in this matter than has Canada.
This is one reason I was very concerned by the attitude of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) when he returned from Europe at the time of the crisis involving the franc and the mark and suggested to the Canadian people that this was really a European problem which did not relate to the Canadian dollar. It is very true that the Canadian dollar was not under attack at that time but it is most unfortunate when the Minister of Finance suggests to the people of Canada, either intentionally or otherwise, that we ought not to be seriously concerned about developments which profoundly affect another country. Anyone who knows what we went through last winter must be very conscious of the danger which may result to Canada from these crises wherever they may develop in the world.
I realize that the influence of Canada is necessarily limited. We are only one country and not the largest in the world in terms of population and influence. I realize that achieving better arrangements represents a very complicated and protracted task. I know something about the time it took to achieve international agreement between the major countries on the matter we now have under consideration, the creation of increased drawing rights. The complexity, the difficulty and the length of time involved in reaching such agreements are however, all the more reason for Canada to be pushing as hard as it can and giving whatever leadership we can in emphasizing the inadequacy of the present arrangements and working for the necessary improvements. The length of time required, plus the obvious dangers with which we are confronted, makes it imperative that we view our situation realistically, that we realize that we and other countries, perhaps Canada in particular, are in a very exposed position. I am not speaking as an alarmist, but I am speaking as one who tries to see the realities as they exist. So I urge the Minister of Finance, the Parliamentary Secretary and the government not to feel for a moment that the measure now before us makes adequate provision to meet the dangers which exist. I urge them to recognize that we do need improved arrangements and that we never know when a crisis will occur. And when it does strike it may hit us a blow which we would find difficult to fend off.
March 7, 1969

For these reasons, since the Minister of Finance is not in the house, I urge the Parliamentary Secretary to bring to the minister's attention the representations I am making today. I urge him and his colleagues to do their best to rally the interest of other countries in this subject and to push forward toward achieving the necessary reforms in international currency arrangements so as to provide us, not with security, because we cannot have security unless we handle our own affairs properly, but at least with a feeling that we shall not constantly be menaced by crises which develop abroad over which we have no control and which we cannot affect through the conduct of our own affairs.

March 7, 1969
Finance
minutes that the United States dollar is the strongest currency by far in the world at large. I also want to draw attention to the fact that too often if we think of the international monetary system purely in terms of foreign exchange we may be overlooking one of the most important things as far as Canada is concerned. I refer to the net debt position of Canada in holdings of foreign assets.
Part of the problem of dealing with the sophisticated area of international finance is a problem of language. This can also be associated with ideas of mystery, gnomes of Zurich, stealthy, shadowy characters and speculators, particularly when one refers to gold standards, gold exchange standards, which followed the gold standard, and convertibility, hot money and cool bankers, floating rates and sinking funds, runs on the pound and crawling pegs, billions and bullion. To most of the public these are terms which do not inform or illuminate.
Let us examine in a few minutes, if we may, some of the fundamental transactions which occur in the international foreign exchange system. It seems to me we are concerned primarily with three types of transaction. We are concerned with transactions which relate to financing of foreign trade. We are concerned with those things which I referred to earlier, the financing and handling of short-term capital flows, and we are equally concerned with the financing of long-term capital flows.
The financing of foreign trade is of particular importance to Canada. Last year Canadian exports rose to a record level. They increased by 19 per cent over the previous year. Canadian exports reached the unprecedented figure of $13,576 million. This put exports on a per capita basis somewhere around $650 per person in Canada. In other words, the exports Canada makes are equivalent to $650 for every person in the country. This shows enormous improvement in foreign trade by our country. This is important to a far greater extent relatively to Canada than to the United States where their exports are roughly 4 per cent of the gross national product compared with the Canadian figure which is close to 20 per cent.
What are the foreign exchange reserves which are used to finance this movement of capital in respect of the trading account, short term or long term? Essentially, up to now they have been two, gold reserves and what are called reserve currencies. The reason for the S.D.R.'s is that international liquidity as reflected by these two units, that

is gold and reserve currencies-primarily United States dollars

has not been expanding very quickly. Gold, for instance, has hardly expanded at all. The gold supply in international affairs for handling international transactions is of the order of about $40 billion. This has increased since 1950 by about $6 billion and has since tapered off. Reserve currencies, primarily United States dollars, have risen. That is to say, the holdings by other countries of United States obligations increased from $5.4 billion in 1950 to $18.3 billion in 1967. This is an increase of some $13 billion. The major part of the increase in world liquidity for the last 15 to 20 years has been provided by an increase in the gold supply of $6 billion and an increase in United States obligations of $13.5 billion. This is roughly $20 billion out of a total increase of close to $24 billion.
The United States has made it clear it is not prepared to increase its obligations abroad at the rate it has in the past. As I indicated already, the gold supply has not been increasing relatively in recent years. If we are going to finance more world trade on trading account we are going to require a new unit. This is what the special drawing right is designed to do.
Let us look then at the question of the intermediate, that is to say, the short-term massive flows which have been destabilizing the system, and which I think will continue to act as destabilizers. There is no question but that this will continue and I see no way of preventing it. We have to recognize that the frequency of short-term massive flows will grow because the relative positions of some countries will diminish through lack of productivity, lack of will, mismanagement or inflation. Their foreign exchange positions are likely to degenerate into deficits in their balance of payments. Those who are interested will start to speculate against the exchange value of that currency.
Similarly, in recent years, particularly within the last year, one can see the effect of unexpected disaster and I refer particularly to the situation in France-the student riots which stimulated or generated the situation we see in France today and about which the rest of the world is jumpy. One of the prime reasons for the current nervousness in the international monetary system, which we have noted within the last two days, is the apparent unwillingness of labour unions to accept the suggestion put to them by their leaders. In other words, there is an increasing
March 7, 19G9

Finance
lack of confidence in the ability of France to manage its economy and retain the value of its exchange rate. At the same time the economies of other countries may grow stronger. This will happen because countries like Germany will grow faster for some of the reverse reasons I have already mentioned- better management, better technology and perhaps fortuitous circumstances. We are going to see a change between the relative positions of countries throughout the world. This will always result in speculation by those who are looking ahead in respect of the effect on the exchange value of the currency.
e (12:30 p.m.)
As we have seen, there has been an unwillingness throughout history, certainly postwar history, on the part of various countries of the world to adjust their exchange rates, as the original I.M.F. provisions anticipated, on a more gradual basis. The original figure was 10 per cent. Very few countries took advantage of this and in many cases went beyond the 10 per cent in the first bite. This has had a destabilizing effect.
Listening to the remarks of the hon. member for Waterloo (Mr. Saltsman), I was curious about his views on the floating exchange rate and how it might serve to solve some of these problems. It was a rather curious, tentative flirtation, it seemed to me. Each time he came close to his subject, each time he was just about to embrace her, he backed off and said that what we really need to do is talk about it some more.
I have referred to the short-term swings, the fact that there will almost inevitably be speculation against the rate because there will be changes occurring as between countries, the unexpected disaster aspect, possibly war, and the temporary measures that may be introduced by governments such as those introduced a little over a year ago by the United States government.
I refer now to the guidelines and to the effects of direct investment. There has been an enormous increase in foreign holdings throughout the world, that is to say, holdings by countries in the fixed assets of other countries. This has been associated with the growth of the multi-national firm. With this growth one can see that there is likely to be greater opportunity for short-term swings as far as capital flows are concerned, because the multi-national firm itself, the international firm itself, will become an agent of moving funds to protect its interests.
As I said earlier, we have seen the defensive actions taken by governments trying to prop up their balance of payments positions by increasing interest rates. This undoubtedly will continue, and undoubtedly we will see more interest arbitrage in years to come. I am trying to emphasize that I think this is the kind of world to which we must adjust ourselves. I do not think we will find easy or quick solutions. I believe we will have to continue to rely on bilateral arrangements, on massive standby credits, and in particular on the enormous strength of the United States foreign assets position. I would like to refer to that for a moment.
In 1950 the United States net external assets were $14 billion, that is to say, United States residents owned abroad $14 billion of assets more than others owned of assets within the United States. By 1966 this figure had risen to $52 billion. I am not including their gold position in this figure. This was a net increase of $38 billion in the foreign holdings of the United States. They financed this in part by a decrease in their gold supply, that is, they sold off approximately $10 billion, and by increasing their obligations in U.S. dollars. With this kind of net position abroad they are in a position at any time, through their corporations, to raise foreign exchange in very much the same way as when a company is short of liquid capital, working capital, it can raise a mortgage against its assets.
Too often we are reminded that the United States is in a deficit position in regard to its current account. It is. The United States, because it has sold off a large part of its gold holdings, because it has increased its foreign obligations, is in deficit by $3.5 billion. In the United Kingdom the figure is a little higher. But both these nations have substantial foreign holdings in fixed form. I suggest that their position is not nearly as serious as it might first appear, if we recognize this strength in behind. For instance, if the United States, as it has been doing, sells its gold, a non-revenue producing asset, to invest in new technology in Europe, surely the United States and the United States dollar are more secure, not less.
I would now like to turn to the position of Canada in the same context. We have foreign exchange reserves of the order of $2.6 billion. They have varied between $2.5 billion and $2.8 billion and may go higher as a result of certain understandings arrived at between Canada and the United States not long ago. I am concerned about the fact that we are likely to become so concerned about the level of

March 7, 1969
Finance
our foreign exchange reserves that we will overlook one of the most important figures to Canada and Canadians. I am referring to the Canadian external assets and liabilities account and the increase in our net deficit position from $4 billion to $24 billion.
In 1949 Canadians owned foreign assets, assets abroad, of $5.3 billion, and foreigners owned in Canada $9.3 billion; in other words, others owned $4 billion more of us than we owned of them collectively. By 1907, according to the latest estimates I have, we increased our assets position by $10 billion; in other words, Canadian holdings abroad increased from slightly over $5 billion to $15 billion. At the same time, our liabilities, that is to say, what others owned of Canada, increased from $9.3 billion to $39 billion, an increase of the order of about $30 billion.
This is the mathematical reflection of the foreign ownership argument, the foreign investment argument, about which we have heard a great deal. I am sure we will hear still more about it. In my view, the fact that others own $24 billion more of us than we own of others collectively, and the fact that this has been increasing year by year, is of major concern to Canada and Canadians.
The classical economic argument was that the young country would be a debtor country but as it developed its own, infant industries, as it developed its own technology, it would break out of the debtor position and become a creditor nation. This was associated, and I think still is associated in many minds today, with Canada contributing to the under developed countries. But we are $24 billion in deficit on our foreign assets account. If we are to make major investments in the underdeveloped world we will have to find ways that we have not yet found of increasing our own wealth.
[DOT] (12:40 p.m.)
In closing I would like to emphasize that the special drawing rights are not a solution to the major problem that we have, that is, the control and understanding of short-term capital flows, but they do indicate an interest and an awareness on the part of the international community in dealing with this prob-em. They represent a very useful enterprise in co-operation on the economic front. To that extent, and to the extent that they impose disciplines on surplus nations and disciplines on deficit nations which use the S.D.R.'s they are a significant contribution to the stability of the international monetary system. We

have to recognize that there will be recurring crises. I think we should be encouraged by the fact that the United States dollar, which is the keystone of the system, is very much stronger than it appears to be, and on the other hand Canadians have to face up to the question that their deficit is increasing. We have not arrested it; it is still continuing, and each time we make ourselves more vulnerable because if at any time those who have invested in Canada decide they want to repatriate their money, to that extent they put the Canadian dollar under pressure.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak on this bill may I say first of all that I support it. I would like to make a few brief comments on the international money system and a few suggestions as to avenues that we might explore as a nation to help in the recurring monetary crises. I am sure all of us know that it has been a bad year for the international payments system. First we had sterling devaluation, then the gold crisis and the introduction of a two-tier price for gold, and then massive speculation stemming from the belief that the mark would be revalued and the franc devalued. I have not included the so-called Canadian dollar crisis last winter because it was not in reality a crisis at all. At that time the United States spending guidelines for American corporations which were extended to subsidiaries operating in Canada caused an air of panic in the Canadian government which was both unseemly and unnecessary. A repetition of those events must be avoided at all costs.
The most recent crisis, however, has been exceptional in its sudden onset, in the degree of international disagreement it has revealed, and in its likely political and economic consequences. The immediate starting point was the political difficulties in France last spring where stability was restored by another inflationary push to the economy. France has pursued a policy of economic expansion reinforced by substantial drawings from the International Monetary Fund. Confidence in the monetary system was not forthcoming.
Germany played a crucial role in these events. It is unfortunate that our government was in hiding as our strong balance of payments position could have enabled us to participate fully in a restructured international monetary system. The franc crisis accelerated the trend toward tax increases and trade restrictions. It might be added that our intervention, if indeed there was any, was singularly unproductive. The policies that
March 7, 1969

were announced were greeted with consternation in many quarters.
The immediate question is: Will the measures be sufficient to preserve the system? Only time will tell, but few observers believe that the conference proposals have much chance of success. If this view is correct, will the revisions of the Bretton Woods Agreements Act as outlined in Bill C-138 solve our problems? Some particular tensions could be healed, but the important fact is that an imaginative approach is lacking. Political leadership appears to be lacking here. This will have important consequences, such as speeding up the attempt to enter the European Common Market with further harm to our export potentials.
It is clear, however, that major reforms can no longer be delayed in the international payments position. The United States played a less dominant role than usual recently because of the interregnum following the American election. This should have presented Canada with a greater opportunity to submit some bright new ideas.
Bill C-138 provides for special drawing rights. These apparently are allocated according to the size of each country's international monetary subscription without any further outlining of objectives. These special drawing rights provide additional lending power. The lending power that is created in this way should be used creatively, possibly in conjunction with World Bank loans or the International Development Association, or perhaps as part of a price stabilization program for primary products. This could be a big help to Canada where various products are subject to international price competition, and therefore this is something that we should push.
Some change in the American approach to the price of gold cannot be ruled out. More radical are other ideas, such as to allow greater exchange rates flexibility by using perhaps the so-called "crawling peg".
The proposed legislation could be improved in other ways too. There must be a better way to combat currency speculation.
The interrelationship of trade and aid is well known, and the dependence of our economy on exports makes it logical that we should try to think ahead, to be more pragmatic and to exert our influence in a constructive fashion. One of our problems will be to restore confidence to the international trading community.
The present policies do not have much chance of success over the long run. If this
Finance
view is correct, it would be appropriate for Canada to be in the forefront of change and to suggest those policies which would be in our interest as long as they are consonant with the interests of the major powers. It might be added that there is little evidence that we have anyone standing up for Canada in these discussions.
May I close by saying that I feel this bill is a step in the right direction but that much more needs to be done.

Mr. Speaker, I believe that Bill C-138 lacks certain features. Today as never before we need new leadership in this field. After all, it is more than a generation since we instituted major reforms in our monetary system. The opposition is often erroneously scorned for its lack of constructive proposals, but I think it is a well known human failing that one blames others for one's own faults. In general I believe this bill should be approved. However, I would like to re-emphasize the words of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) that international monetary systems, no matter how well they function, will not take the place of well directed domestic and trade policies within the country itself.
Most people who have thought about and studied the international monetary system agree that there is need to enlarge the world's monetary reserves, and there is no easy or simple solution to our problems in this field. For example, merely increasing the price of gold would not really solve anything. At this time we must find new solutions to new problems when the leadership and system that have been wanting must be replaced by a new point of view.
For example, the special drawing rights created by this agreement can best function if they are allied with all the reserve assets of the various participating nations. Each country could earmark part of its reserves to this new fund but would retain title to them. If Canada put in $800 million in gold, $1 billion in dollars and $500 million in special drawing rights, it would have a total credit of $2.3 billion. It could use this reserve to settle its account and would use its reserve assets in the proportion earmarked.
[DOT] (12:50 p.m.)
Again, it seems that this reserve fund could be used productively. The mere existence of an important reserve balance would enable us to put a larger percentage of our foreign exchange reserves into, for example, an aid

March 7, 1969
Finance
program to the Colombo group. Our foreign exchange fund of $2.5 billion was inadequate a year ago, but it was supplemented by I.M.F. credits. If reserve assets were placed in a new organization, a greater proportion of those assets could be put to work in some constructive enterprise.
It has been suggested that there should be a better way of dealing with sudden capital movements in various markets such as brought about the quick flight of capital from Canada a year ago. There should be new methods to offset destabilizing but reversible short-term capital movements. Last year we had to appeal to Washington to amend its guidelines with regard to United States corporations operating in Canada. It would have been a lot less demeaning had there been some international assistance on which to call. The International Monetary Fund eventually provided us with credits, but we had to make urgent pleas to the United States first. Reserves had to be borrowed in Europe and in the United States, and subsequently our bank rate was raised to 7J per cent and the money supply was tightened. These moves, of course, hurt business activity.
Perhaps we could assist in establishing regional arrangements under the umbrella of an over-all I.M.F. system. Caribbean countries would welcome something along this line. The more these nations are helped to establish their credit, the greater the trading opportunities for us. The developing Commonwealth countries would buy more if they could obtain credits and if their currencies were more solidly established. The great resources of the free world are not in doubt. All that is needed is their effective utilization, and we must now think about taking a few steps in that direction.
Most economists now call for greater flexibility in determining exchange rates. Fixed exchange rates are not fixed forever, of coruse. All that happens is that the changes, when they occur, are bigger than they would be if there were a 1 per cent or 2 per cent annual adjustment. This kind of compromise would allow for gradual changes to take place. None would be so drastic that they could not be offset by changes in interest rates, which would prevent the flow of funds out of one country. If exchange rates varied, say, one twelfth of one per cent per month or 1 per cent per year, speculators would probably decide that currency raids were not worth the trouble. It would cost exporters and importers a little more to protect forward commitments if currencies were allowed to 
fluctuate by wider margins, but many major balance of payments disturbances could be avoided by permitting wider spreads in currency values. If speculative incentives were removed, Canada would not be so compelled to change its interest levels, regardless of the effect upon its domestic policies, in order to meet situations created by the demands of foreign creditors.
United strength has kept the free world strong and productive. The important question now is whether we can make some necessary changes. If we fail to rise to the challenge we shall only ensure that our problems will grow, and it will become more difficult later to find a way forward. I see little evidence in the bill before us of the new look necessary to ensure progress and stability.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in the discussion on Bill C-138 providing for amendments to the Bretton Woods Agreements and other legislation.
Many things could be said on this subject. We had even contemplated introducing amendments but due to the international nature of this legislation which has been prepared in advance by experts in international finance, it is rather difficult for any one in a government such as ours to propose amendments. However, we should be benefiting from these agreements as we are participating in them. However, the main features have been established by the world's higher financial authorities and it is rather difficult to propose an amendment intended to reconcile the requirements of human beings and those of industry.
Therefore, such being the case, we will have to be satisfied in commenting on the general aspects of the bill and analyzing its impact on Canadians. What are the advantages to be gained by these improvements, by changes brought about by the large financial institutions?
Mr. Speaker, it is our opinion that the suggested improvements are nothing but haphazard solutions. This legislation will not cure the ills. It could delay their aggravation or diminish their effects temporarily, but the consequences are nevertheless unavoidable, until some day the situation becomes worse than ever.
[DOT] (2:10 p.m.)
In respect of debt repudiation, we have not seen the last of that. The results of these economic ills will be delayed by this sugar-coated pill prepared for us by high international finance, which we will have to swallow in spite of ail our objections. Canada could surely get out of these agreements if its economy and financial status were sound. In fact, some countries do not need them to
finance their operations, and they live just the same and even trade with other countries. We are a member of that organization, and should any difficulties arise in this country, we could get a sugar-coated pill to delay the progress of the disease. That will not remove the effects of the disease. Indeed, we shall have to put up with them later and it is just a question of time.
Mr.. Speaker, the world is always on the move, going through the failures and successes of the great international wars which are, as it were, serious surgical operations that are none the less the strong evidence of a surprising vitality and even of a better recovery.
In 1944, at the end of the war, when one could expect that it would wind up successfully for the allied powers, financial experts from all parts of the world met in Bretton Woods, in New Hampshire and laid the groundwork for postwar international operations. After long discussions, it was decided to establish the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development and the International Monetary Fund. This was considered as an economic and not a political system. Russia sent non-participating observers, because she did not want to be considered a capitalist country. She wished to retain her Communist or socialist philosophy, which of course differs from capitalism or economic liberalism.
Mr. Speaker, we are in 1969, 25 years after the Breton Woods Agreements. A quarter of a century has elapsed since those famous meetings where the great bankers of the capitalist countries laid the foundations of an international monetary system. We must reflect on the happy or unhappy results of the structures of those organizations, on their qualities which must be preserved and their weaknesses must be eliminated.
Mr. Speaker, in short, those institutions were useful and even necessary. The experience of 25 years can be very instructive and reassuring for all countries. I think the International Bank and the International Monetary Fund are necessary and must be maintained. We must study closely their mechanism with a view to improving it and making it more effective as well as more accessible to the countries which cannot benefit from it, even though they are members.
Whatever the differences, Mr. Speaker, which seem to exist between the various currencies, as well as between various methods of administration and various economic philosophies, political economy is based upon

March 7. 1969
Finance
the same needs, the same requirements and the same imperatives.
Everywhere, Mr. Speaker, the production oi goods and services is made by adults, for the whole population. That production has two purposes: consumption of those goods and services by the whole population, and capitalization of surpluses to ensure future production as well as the development of production, producing instruments and constant productivity for a progressive national and international population.
Everywhere, Mr. Speaker, we find that production equals consumption and capitalization. Whether in a capitalist, socialist or Communist country, everywhere the production of goods and services is made for consumption and capitalization by adults and by the whole population.
Thus, a distinction should be made between monetary, economic and political systems. This new distinction, at least for persons who are not aware of the great international principles, can be very useful to understand what appears to be so complicated when money is mentioned in our economic and political discussion's.
Everyone knows that production is achieved through capital and labour, and that capital deserves a wage, an interest, if it is reasonable. The resulting buying power is then used to purchase a share of the output. All that is part and parcel of an economic system, of an international banking system or of the Bretton Woods Agreements, if you want. That is one aspect of the present economy. A distinction has to be made between the monetary system and economics.
In July 1942, the end of the war was felt to be near. The larger countries had an eye on the post-war period and were planning whatever orientation might be given to the international economy, by means of super-national agencies. In Bretton Woods, in 1944, the question was not to create the United Nations Organization but to organize the financial affairs of the capitalist nations. The point was not international policies but international finance. The two subjects are always treated separately even though financiers and statesmen of national or international standing are often the same people.
It must be understood and recognized that all those organizations are a far cry from the small enterprise and oblivious to the needs of the individuals and their families. Financial delegates or members of this great institution are only concerned with big problems.

At such a high level, that of the large undertakings, only capital and capital gains are protected and promoted. The individual, the family, the farm and the small industry are completely disregarded at the meetings of that institution. At that stage, only the mil-lionnaires in countries belonging to international institutions take part in the discussions.
[DOT] (2:20 p.m.)
One has to realize that the delegates to such great exhibitions of international financial know-how get quickly into the habit of talking in millions of dollars and easily forget the problems of cents, dollars, work, family budget, purchasing power, unemployment, social or family allowances.
Even if Mr. Deutsch resumed his post from 1963 to 1968 as president of the Economic Council of Canada, he is already used to great financial ways, to financial and international theories and principles. Even if Mr. Rasminsky became later Governor of the Bank of Canada he is already more concerned with millions and billions rather than with the needs of small institutions, families and small industries in Canada, because large businesses seem able to draw his attention. Those big shots are managing the economy of the country with a mind opened to the consideration of large projects rather than the needs of the individuals and the family. This is why I say that Mr. Rasminsky has no qualms about increasing the rates of the Bank of Canada when it suits him or the great powers, even if it is prejudicial to the nation. As Governor of the Bank of Canada, he has the power to do it and no economist or official of the present government can intervene, not even the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson).
We must understand them and leave them to their elaborate explanations, but we must develop another argumentation from the bottom, to get to the needs of families, small family businesses, farms, stores, still the most important part of the population, without which there would be no country to sign the Bretton Woods Agreements.
If the large institutions handle millions and billions of dollars accumulated through profits, and reserve capital, it must be borne in mind that their importance is due precisely to the great many small employees, the millions of salaried workers who administer family budgets.
Among the great Canadians present at Bretton Woods were the right hon. Louis St-Laurent, then Minister of Justice and later Prime Minister of Canada, the hon. Lio-
March 7, 1969

nel Chevrier, Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Munitions and Supply and later Chairman of the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority, Mr. G. F. Towers, then Governor of the Bank of Canada, who remained in that office until 1955, Mr. J. J. Deutsch, Assistant to the Secretary of State for External Affairs, who was to become later the Chairman of the Economic Council of Canada in 1963, Mr. Louis Rasminsky, deputy chairman of the Central Council of the Foreign Exchange Board, who became governor of the Bank of Canada. It will be noted that all these great Canadians, like all the great financiers and politicians of other countries who were present when the Bretton Woods Agreements were signed, stood aloof from individual and family problems and were deeply interested in matters of millions and billions of dollars with which important national and international institutions are able to deal.
When they founded the International Bank and the International Monetary Fund at Bretton Woods in 1944, the least of their concerns was the protection of the individual and of the family within which the individual can grow.
It must therefore be understood, Mr. Speaker, that on that solemn occasion when the Bretton Woods Agreements were negotiated, the participants were thinking big, they were thinking in terms of millions and billions and not in terms of the cents and dollars of the citizens of Canada and other countries.
In 1944, when soldiers fell every day by the thousands on the battlefields, the importance of the individual was certainly the least worry of politicians and bankers, whether national or international.
Capital and its relevant institutions claimed all the efforts of the learned men assembled at Bretton Woods.
The idea was to place international organizations above even the most powerful and prosperous national organizations belonging to the 44 countries represented there.
Such was the spirit pervading the minds of politicians and financial leaders of the greatest countries in the world. So they set up an International Monetary Fund, and an International Bank which, in fact, are hardly anything else but extensions of national, financial and banking organizations. Such are the broad lines; details are irrelevant.
There is no use asking those huge organizations to save the individual human being, who is bom and raised only too often unfortunately in slums.
Finance
You will notice that politicians, businessmen and bankers of high national and international standing are all university graduates so they cannot help doing what they were taught to do at the university. When they realize that their great distinction leaves behind them and their mighty organizations such dismal failures as unbalanced economies or wide gaps between the rich who go on growing richer and the poor who sink ever deeper in poverty and destitution, here is their excuse: We have to act according to what we learned at the university.
From the political, financial, economic and banking points of view, the basic training is dispensed by the same central universities, English, European or American; they teach the same political philosophy, the same techniques and the same doctrines.
The universities of Oxford, Paris, Louvain, Rome, Harvard, M.I.T., which our Canadian, European and American economists attended, teach, discuss and dialogue in the same way on all financial and economic matters.
Mr. Speaker, it is almost unbelievable. In the smallest parish, where there is a credit union, or the branch office of a bank, you will find, even if it is on a small scale, the monetary, economic and political mechanisms found on an international scale in Bretton Woods, the International Monetary Fund and the International Bank.
Whether we study the infinitely small or the infinitely large, our world is so well made, so well adjusted that we find the same phenomena, the same problems, the same solutions, the same difficulties, the same research and the same conclusions.
Everywhere money is a means of exchange controlled by the financial and economic powers that be, the great world bankers. They control the economic blood of the nation.

subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND AND EXCHANGE FUND ACCOUNT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if I understood correctly, I am asked whether an international capitalistic system can exist without the Bretton Woods agreements?

March 7. 1963
Finance
I shall say yes. We could denounce those agreements. All we would have to do then is to restore the balance in our national economy.
[DOT] (2:30 p.m.)
But we participate in them, because it is some kind of assurance taken for fear of future events. Since we are afraid to find ourselves in a bad position, we are participants in the Bretton Woods Agreements. We realize this is not a proper solution, but it is our belief that we can thus be assured of some protection and that we will be in a position to assist other countries which are in a similar situation. Through co-operation, those countries which are better off economically and which have signed those agreements will be able to help other countries whose economy is less well balanced.
In my opinion, those are so many reasons which explain our participation in the Bretton Woods Agreements.
Mr. Speaker, everything is on the move, production, consumption and capitalization. However, some balance and harmony should also be found everywhere. It is no more difficult to achieve this balance both on the national and the international levels than on the personal, family, municipal, provincial or federal levels. Those three national, international or world levels really exist, in a quite different way, indeed, but always according to the same laws and principles. It is a matter of economic and political administration through money, capital and credit where there is trust among fellow-men. Man is the basic element of this problem. Man is always the origin of financial transactions involving millions and billions of dollars on the national, international or world levels.
In short, considering the world history and the history of money, I heartily rejoice in the present world situation of 1969.
Some twenty five years after the Bretton Woods Agreements and the end of World War II, we can see much progress in the world. I think it is proper to say again that even though we did not have at our disposal the economic tools capable of being most helpful for high financial institutions which were more or less accessible to the people, who could not derive full benefit from them, our capitalistic system is still the best in the world. It is up to us to maintain it because as compared to the socialist or communist systems, we see

that our capitalism has a right to exist, providing we correct the abuses it allows sometimes.
When the United States succeed in sending three cosmonauts around the moon, and when Russia succeeds in coupling two Soyouz and cosmonauts in outer space, such accomplishments show the kind of progress, evolution and development achieved by the human race. And this is only the beginning of the fantastic developments expected before long. But let us come back to our monetary, economical and political problems. Man is the source of all activities, national as well as international. Instead of criticizing our monetary, economic, political and university systems, let us be happy about these marvelous accomplishments, and let us work with confidence towards the improvement of some simple details overlooked by higher authorities, overconcerned with the establishment of international organizations.
One should not blame the monetary, economic and political systems. They must be criticized if they do not operate with the greatest efficiency expected. However, all organizations are operating better and better and with more and more efficiency. Now, we must make them operate fully, with the utmost efficiency in the smallest detail as far as individual and family needs are concerned. There is abundance for all. The individual and the universal are one and the same thing. Millions and billions should not make us overlook cents and dollars. In my opinion, that is how we should first consider the Bretton Woods Agreements.
Even if, at the present time, we have not been able to improve that very complicated legislation already prepared by the great international financial organizations, yet we have something to say to influence our representatives and the leaders of the country. We must ask them to consider not only the great problems but also the lesser ones. There are minor urgent problems that must be settled. However, only great problems are dealt with, for the benefit of great institutions. Smaller institutions must also be helped. In my opinion, we are responsible for trying to influence our representatives who are negotiating the Bretton Woods Agreements.
Mr. Speaker, it is in that way that we will be able to achieve something. It is not by getting rid of everything good, because what is good should remain. It is not by destroying that we will build. We must build, but it is forbidden to destroy.
March 7, 1969

Established in 1944 through the Bretton Woods Agreements, the International Monetary Fund and the International Bank are now 25 years old. Both institutions have had significant effects. They did much more through their activities and the central leadership given to member States in the postwar period than if every country had been left on its own, without any guidelines.
The Monetary Fund and the International Bank have at least created a climate of confidence between small and great nations, between the war-torn countries which had to rebuild everything, and the countries which were spared massive destruction and we were able to co-operate, according to a definite plan, to the reconstruction and the development of devastated countries.
That those institutions have been beneficial to the most powerful of the member countries, and that others benefited less, that remains to be ascertained. Some improvements could be brought about if necessary but on the whole, the existence of those institutions has been greatly justified and much appreciated by all.
The unrest which persists in some countries can be corrected in the long run, and the weaknesses of those institutions may be remedied to ensure an even greater efficiency and benefit to all countries concerned, and even to the whole world.
The uneasiness at the heart of certain international financial organizations is similar in nature to the deficiencies which appear in the monetary, political or economic systems of countries, provinces, cities and villages. The powerful help the less fortunate, but demand to profit from it, which is normal and profitable for all concerned, large and small alike. Profit is necessary to all, but the essential thing is to bring about a certain balance between the participants. Proportion, balance, and harmony, all are needed. One must live and give to each according to his talents and his needs. We, who are strong, must help those who are not as yet. Let us help each other, for we are all friends and brothers, and we all have the same Father.
That is what we must strive to achieve, at the level of international institutions, as well as at the national, federal, provincial, regional, community, family, social, personal, and individual level.
All individuals and all nations are interdependent. The entire world is made up of human beings living on earth. Unrest between countries or citizens of the same country are
Finance
always due to a lack of proportion, balance and harmony. All those qualities are within the scope of the human mind, according to the capacity of human beings managing different institutions.
Normally, it should not be more difficult for the Minister of Finance to balance his revenues, expenditures and profits in his national budget than for the president of the Royal Bank of Canada to balance the balance-sheet of his bank or the head of a family to balance the family budget, always according to the same sound formula: administration, revenues, expenditures and profits.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
When there is abundance and over abundance for all, but some make excessive profits compelling others to show deficits prejudicial to good administration and understanding, the proportion, balance and harmony are destroyed. Whether at the individual, municipal, family or international level, those imbalances must be eliminated.
To maintain the balance of international economy the economic flow between those nations must be abundant and sufficient, because if the economic pressure exerted by institutions is too great, societies will be in a bad way and unbalanced.
On the other hand, if the economy of a country is too weak, new blood must be injected to bring about economic stability, in much the same way it is done to improve the circulation in a human body. The person who suffers from high blood pressure must get a treatment likely to lower the blood pressure. But in cases of low blood pressure, tonics must be prescribed in order to restore normal conditions, and enable the person to be active and enjoy life again.
Mr. Speaker, the same holds true in respect of national or international finance. Our economy lacks stability. In fact, some people get too much profit at the expense of others. Some people are poor because others make excessive profits. That is what is happening at both the international and national levels.
Mr. Speaker, we should try to get those things through to our distinguished university people who can improve and stabilize the world or our national economy. I have not enough connections to contact them but government members are powerful enough; they can bring forth the necessary arguments and they should think about the country. The national economy must be stabilized so that

March 7, 1969
Finance
we can finally enjoy a perfect system which will develop to help the people and do away with the dissatisfaction and the disasters we experience today.
We must all assume our responsibilities in this respect. As far as I am concerned, I am prepared to assume my responsibility. If I were influential enough to wind my way among the participants in the negotiations on the Bretton Woods Agreements and try to make them understand my ideas, I would do it. However, I am only a member of the opposition, but common sense tells me that in spite of a lack of balance, the existing system is good. Therefore it must be retained. Capitalism is the best system in the world, it is its abuses which must be corrected. It is those abuses which are putting our economies out of balance and this explains why damage is done. We do not know the cause for the present financial uneasiness. To put an end to that uneasiness, we must remove the cause. There is always one. As long as we do not endeavour to remove the causes, we will not have settled the problem.
As to international drawing rights they are new credits which banks will be able to issue at will; the banks will issue international credits exactly as national banks are now issuing credits within their own countries. This was not done previously. It is somewhat an improvement inasmuch as it is better than nothing. However, then again, it will not solve the problem because if we are going to issue credit bearing interest, the latter will not be created at the same time. Reimbursement of credits which have been issued, plus reimbursement of interest which has not been issued will be required. This may lead, later, to a national unbalance. There still will be repudiation of debts, because we have not found the real solution to the problem.
If debt free credits had been issued, a solution to the problem would have been found, but since these new credits will run every country into debt, they will enable international bankers to take over the assets of a country. Then, one day, that country will be unable to make its payments because it will not be able to give back more than it has received, and its economy will lose its balance. From an international point of view, it is simply a time bomb given to the nations.
Again, these new credits do not constitute the real solution to the problem we should correct, but if one does not have any bread, one eats something else. This legislation is put to us all prepared in advance by these great institutions, and there is nothing we can say.
[Mr. Latulippe.l
We want to bring forward some changes, but we know that nothing will be changed. We have discussed that in committee where the bill was considered clause by clause. I asked some questions and big financiers answered that the unbalanced economic situ-aion that we know at this time, as well as the repudiations of debts we have already known, will not be eliminated. There will be more repudiations of debts. That was recognized in committee. We discussed and scrutinized this problem. I am convinced there is not much that can be changed. However, we should remain firm in our convictions.
