speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my remarks will be short and very much to the point. If hon. members have not realized it already, it is high time we came to the conclusion that just patching the crutches of present international monetary policy is not good enough. All Bill C-138 does is further extend the Bretton Woods Agreement as it applies to international financing. The needs of the international monetary situation in relation to both the developed and underdeveloped countries deserve something far more lasting and permanent than this.
It seems to me that we have no alternative at this time but to support Bill C-138. Again I say it is impossible to continue patching up the old system while at the same time thinking it is going to serve us very much longer. We can have no better example of this than the situation involving the French franc at this very moment. France is in difficulty in this regard and every nation in the free world is concerned, because no nation can stand alone on monetary policy in this time of freer trade when trade is so desperately important.
e (2:50 p.m.)
A few months ago Canada was in difficulties. At the present time our dollar is reasonably stable and our international credits are not in too bad a condition. But in view of what is happening on the world monetary scene, this condition is temporary. The American dollar is in difficulty; the British pound is in difficulty. As long as we countenance this situation we are hastening the -day of reckoning. The situation will then be all
March 7, 1969

the more difficult because a more realistic *approach was not taken to this problem.
I think Canada should be doing something to improve the situation. We are in a very favourable position to take the lead in this matter. In the Committee of Ten, which is conducting a continuing study of international monetary policies, Canada should take the lead and bring forward forthright and realistic reforms that will cause the entire monetary picture to be effective so far as the needs of the world are concerned.
Not too long ago, when studying the economic problems of some of the developing nations, I realized that the chronic deficit in the balance of international payments situation of the underdeveloped countries is such that it is increasingly difficult for these countries to even repay their obligations to the World Bank. Therefore this problem affects the underdeveloped nations as well.
One of the great needs in the international monetary area is greater liquidity. Only if we have this liquidity can we effect the transfer of those things that enter into the over-all aspect of international trade and international settlements. There is today very little support for replacing the existing system and beginning a new arrangement; therefore we continue as we have in the past, trying to fill the gaps and plug the holes in the World Bank and in the arrangements that came out of the international agreement at Bretton Woods. Therefore, the problem is forever with us.
It seems to me that one of the great needs on the international scene today is for a bank of international settlements where the problem of gold, its value and repricing could be set aside, because even as the gold standard was inadequate for us 30 years ago the gold standard on the international scene is just as inadequate today. If a bank of international settlements were set up, there could be a much freer settlement of international accounts, which would encourage trade. This would not only make the situation easier for the developing countries but would ease the pressures on the main currencies on the international scene.
My comments are aimed at that single point, Mr. Speaker. While we lend our support to Bill C-138, this is done with full acknowledgement of the fact that all we are doing is further extending a system that has already proven to be inadequate. I hope the government will take advantage of this opportunity to give leadership in the committee of which we are a major member in
Finance
order that a completely new approach may be taken to this whole problem.
The seriousness of the situation is emphasized to us in Canada by reason of the increasing cost of living and the fact that inflation is taking a death grip on our entire economic picture as it is related to other countries of the world with whom we must compete in international trade. The agricultural industry is basically concerned with this problem. Other primary industries are concerned with it. If it were not for the tremendous imbalance of trade that we have with our neighbours across the border, the United States, perhaps we would be forced into a position where we would understand that even Canada, in its favoured position, cannot continue as we are. These few words emphasize the point I am trying to make, Mr. Speaker. I draw to the attention of the house the necessity of a completely new approach in this regard, and I urge the government to take some leadership in the matter.

subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND AND EXCHANGE FUND ACCOUNT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hesitate to follow immediately the free-flowing expertise of the two previous speakers on the subject of international monetary arrangements. However, I should like to address a few words to the subject matter of Bill C-138. Some outspoken members this afternoon have referred to the Bretton Woods Agreement as being nothing but a negative force or institution in the world scene. I take this opportunity to express the conviction that it would be a sad day for the free world, the western world, if we were to lose whatever orderliness we have achieved in the postwar period through international monetary arrangements. I think the communist block would be more than happy to see some kind of departure from international monetary arrangements in the western world, because they hope that sufficient chaos would result to bring about that breakdown in the western capitalist and social democratic systems for which they have long waited. I agree that there are deficiencies in the present arrangements under the Bretton Woods Agreement. Nevertheless, the essence of the agreement is such that we must take the position that it must be reformed gradually and from time to time over the years.
In so far as the specific content of this bill is concerned, having to do with the establishment of special drawing rights, this is a welcome move. My colleague, the late hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands, over

March 7, 1969
Finance
the last three or four years that I recall consistently urged successive ministers of finance to urge on the international monetary negotiators on behalf of Canada just this kind of move, namely, the establishment of special drawing rights. I see the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gray) nodding his head in agreement. I am happy that this much is established. Therefore this move, in so far as it goes, is welcomed.
However, I express disappointment that more fundamental reforms have not been suggested. Perhaps I overestimate the importance of it, but it seems to me that in the course of the last three years we have witnessed enough disequilibrium, enough shake-ups in the currencies of various countries which are party to this agreement, that we can say a malaise exists in the international monetary system.
Something more ought to be done than what is involved in Bill C-138. The creation of special drawing rights is fine. It will add to international liquidity. As has been suggested by previous speakers, the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson) in particular, I think it is generally agreed that as world trade has increased in the past decade there has not been a proportionate increase in the means of settling the accounts involved in international trade. Therefore we welcome the move to increase liquidity by means of special drawing rights.
The question should be asked: Why was not this done sooner? I think the answer lies in the simple fact that there exists in some countries a certain basic, primitive kind of selfishness. Those countries which had a healthy balance of payments situation in previous years were often the ones that opposed any concrete move toward the establishment of special drawing rights. The same countries that opposed it when their balance of payments situation was healthy later supported the establishment of special drawing rights when their balance of payments situation turned negative.
[DOT] (3:00 p.m.)
When the situation became really bad they were the ones to become most active in advocating these special drawing rights. Perhaps it is not important to question motives, but both the United States and France created the most difficulties when special drawing rights were discussed. One of them has certainly come around full face in favour of them and, although I have not had time to

check lately, I suspect that even France has now come around to a rather lukewarm support of S.D.R.
There is another point I wish to express. It seems obvious to me that if national governments are expected to surrender some of their sovereignty in financial and economic affairs for the sake of international orderliness, this is fine. But if national governments are expected to do that, then I suggest that citizens of these nations should likewise be expected to do so. It has always surprised me that some of the countries which are parties to the Bretton Woods Agreements, and to other international monetary arrangements, have never required as a matter of law that their nationals be prohibited from holding gold in private stock.
I believe that some of the bad effects of international monetary speculations have been due in large part to the speculation carried on by private persons with large funds and economic power at their disposal. These people have used their position and privilege to speculate to the detriment of their own country, and of the free world as a whole, because if one country in the free world falls into financial chaos, it follows logically there would be a chain reaction. I do not know why the international monetary authorities have not yet recommended or requested that member national governments take legislative action to prevent or prohibit the holding of gold stocks in private hands.
I was a member of the delegation visiting France last December, and at that time the President of the French Republic took the opportunity to make a lengthy speech on the subject of international monetary arrangements, and of the French currency situation in particular. He certainly did not spare anyone's feelings in condemning the action of private speculators and the detrimental effect they have on their country and on their fellow citizens.
Although I feel that in Bill C-138 we are finally taking the desirable action hoped for in the past five years or more, namely to increase international liquidity by setting up special drawing rights, there are still other even more fundamental things to move toward in international monetary arrangements.
Finally, I should like to refer to something which the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) mentioned, as reported at page 5896 of Hansard for February 24. He was joined by other hon. members, including my colleague, the hon. member for Waterloo (Mr. March 7, 1969

Finance
Saltsman). He spoke about the extent to which a member country of the Bretton Woods Agreement can choose between various kinds of foreign exchange rates. I am not sufficiently expert in the field to be able to make a judgment as to whether free floating exchange rates are preferable as compared to fixed, but it seems to me that when an international monetary arrangement impinges so much on a country's financial affairs that it cannot choose between two different kinds of exchange rates, then perhaps that international agreement is too restrictive. For slightly more than five years, we in Canada have been so rigidly committed to a fixed exchange rate that at times it put us in a nonsensical position, and this has been allowed to continue for too long.
I believe the hon. member for Edmonton West may well have had a point when he suggested that between a rigidly fixed exchange rate on the one hand and, on the other hand, a free floating exchange rate there may well be a common sense, flexible arrangement, namely an exchange rate fluctuating between an upward and a lower limit. This may well be the most sensible course for Canada to adopt. I tend to agree with him and hope that the minister, his parliamentary secretary and those with whom they are associated in the parliamentary committee, will give this suggestion very close consideration.
Mr. H. E. Gray (Parliamentary Secretary to
Minister of Finance):	Mr. Speaker, hon.
members have made many interesting comments, and expecting this to be the case I rose at the opening of this debate on third reading on a point of order to indicate that it was my intention to speak after others had spoken so that I would be able to attempt to respond to at least some of these comments.

I think it would be proper to recall that the object of this bill is to ratify certain amendments to the Bretton Woods Agreements. Those amendments resulted from negotiations during which the representatives of the Canadian people played a most active role. They provide for the creation of special drawing rights.
I must point out to the hon. member for Compton (Mr. Latulippe) that this bill is designed to allow Canada to take part in that program of special drawing rights.

The hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) made some interesting comments about the continuing need for conditional liquidity. I think it should be noted that even with the creation of these special drawing rights, which are a form of unconditional liquidity, there continues to be a place for conditional liquidity. The ability to have increases in this latter sort of liquidity continues to exist through the mechanisms in the International Monetary Fund agreement which makes possible increases in the existing quotas of the members of the I.M.F. In this way, the fund will be able to meet the needs of its members for both types of liquidity.
I was most interested to learn that the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Schreyer) seems to have a greater degree of sympathy for the workings of the Bretton Woods Agreement and the International Monetary Fund than does his colleague, the hon. member for Waterloo (Mr. Saltsman). I think it was very useful for the hon. member for Selkirk to remind the house of the views of the late Colin Cameron, the former member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands, who over the years spoke very strongly in favour of the creation of a form of managed currency in the international field which would be somewhat analogous to the managed currencies which have been created in modern countries of the west.
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)
Certainly, I was concerned to hear what seemed to be an indication from the hon. member for Waterloo of less support for this concept than the late Colin Cameron exhibited. But I was pleased to note the support for it put forward by the hon. member for Selkirk. We should recall that Canada is particularly dependent on the existence of a smoothly operating system of international trade. The hon. member for Waterloo appeared to cast some doubt upon the wisdom of Canada's participation in such a system, but I suggest we cannot expect to enjoy its benefits if we are not prepared to take part in the processes of international negotiation and discussion for its improvement as we have been doing over the years, one result of which is the bill we are now considering. I sincerely hope the hon. member for Waterloo is not seeking a return to the conditions which persisted before the first world war, conditions of autarchy, with

March 7, 1969
Finance
declining world trade and resultant depression and unemployment.
I would point out to the hon. member for Waterloo that contrary to what he appeared to suggest in his remarks, the rules of the fund do not provide for a veto to be held by any one country. Though the size of the quota of the United States gives it a certain weight in voting, the same could be said for the common market countries acting together as they would be able to do under one of the amendments to the fund agreement which we are considering. We should recall that the International Monetary Fund exists not in the interest of any one country but in the interests of its members as a whole.
I should also point out with respect to the ability of member countries to draw what is known as the first tranche that no special conditions have been laid down in advance for so doing, contrary to what was suggested by the hon. member for Waterloo.
The special drawing rights scheme provides a way of supplementing present stocks of international reserves including those which are held in the form of gold at their existing prices. Again, therefore, contrary to what appears to have been suggested by the hon. member for Waterloo, the scheme will not have the effect of doubling the price of gold.
The hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Ritchie) made some interesting comments about the possible uses of the new special drawing rights. It should be remembered that the purpose of creating these rights is to add to the supply of international reserves a form of unconditional liquidity. Once the scheme is in operation participating countries will be able to use these rights without accepting conditions of the type which could be imposed on them in connection with the use of the present rights, the only conditions being the repurchase obligation which I described at an earlier stage of this debate and a further obligation through which participants in the special drawing rights scheme are expected to use those rights basically for balance of payments purposes and not solely to change the condition of the reserves. I should also like to thank the hon. member for Etobicoke (Mr. Gillespie) for his useful and stimulating comments.
The participation of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) in this debate demonstrates how an understanding of the importance to Canada of a smoothly operating monetary system can cut across party lines. I can assure him I shall bring his remarks to

the attention of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson). As he perhaps knows, I am here on behalf of the minister and on his behalf I have had carriage of this piece of legislation from the outset.
I wish to assure the hon. gentleman that the Minister of Finance and the government are following developments on the international monetary scene very closely. The active participation of Canadian representatives in negotiations leading up to the formulation of the special drawing rights scheme, and the present efforts of the government to obtain parliamentary approval for Canada's participation in it show, in my opinion at least, the importance which the government attaches to such matters.
As I pointed out during earlier stages of this bill, the special drawing rights scheme is an important step forward in the development of the international monetary system. As I have said before, and in this I agree with some of the remarks made by other hon. members, it should not be considered to be a panacea or a cure-all for the problems of the international monetary system; there will continue to be problems to be dealt with within the context of that system. Nevertheless, the existence of this scheme will help ensure that the future growth of world trade and payments will not be impeded by a lack of reserves in the system. This is very important to Canada, as the hon. member for Etobicoke pointed out, since we are a major trading nation. Our prosperity-the prosperity of our workers and farmers-depends on world trade to a degree equalled by only a very small number of other countries.
This is why I ask the house for approval of the amendments before us. They represent a package arising from negotiations in which Canadian representatives played a very active part. The passage of this bill will mean that Canada is giving formal agreement to the creation of this special drawing rights scheme as well as an indication that it will be taking part in it.
For the program to come into effect, the amendments to the International Monetary Fund agreement must be accepted by at least three-fifths of the membership of the International Monetary Fund holding at least 80 per cent of the total votes. As of December 31, 1968, 27 countries representing 42.2 per cent of the total votes had given their approval. As of February 13, 1969, 34 members representing 50.51 per cent of the total voting power had accepted the amendment. The minimum number of countries whose support is
March 7, 1969

required for the agreement to come into effect is 67 and Canada's acceptance will add a further 3.2 per cent to the votes. This will not only bring the scheme nearer to adoption but it will, it is hoped, encourage other countries to approve of the scheme coming into existence.
Once the scheme has been accepted by the required majorities it will be possible for the first time for international monetary reserves to be created by deliberate and joint action of the nations belonging to the International Monetary Fund to meet the requirements of the whole international monetary system.
I think most hon. members who participated in the work of the Standing Committee on Finance will agree with me when I say that contrary to what was suggested by the hon. member for Waterloo this bill did receive detailed study there. Serious attention was given to it by members of the committee representing all parties in this house. At the time we seemed to be completing our work, no member of the committee thought it necessary to rise to propose that the study be continued, that witnesses be recalled or that further witnesses be heard. The committee held seven meetings on the bill, earh extending over several hours, and during those meetings it heard evidence from senior officials of the Department of Finance and the Bank of Canada, the men who have represented our country in the negotiations leading to the development of this special drawing rights scheme.
The committee heard the views of economists linked with banks and investment houses on the question of exchange rates and other related aspects of the international monetary system. Members were able to question the witnesses directly on the subject of the bill and related matters in a way which would not have been possible had the bill remained in the committee of the whole house under the old rules in force before the Christmas recess. Therefore, it is my feeling that the opportunities members of the committee had there certainly brought about a broadening of understanding on the part of all who participated in the hearings on the issues and problems connected with international monetary policy.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
In conclusion, let me thank the hon. members who have participated in the discussion of this bill both in the house and in the finance committee. I again ask the house for its
Control of Pesticide Use approval and support of this bill so that we can participate in this special drawing rights scheme which is a step forward in the development of a system of international payments and world trade, something very important for both the present and future prosperity of Canada.
Motion agreed to, bill read the third time and passed.

speechtext: The house resumed, from Friday, February 21, consideration of the motion of Mr. Olson that Bill C-157, to regulate products used for the control of pests and the organic functions of plants and animals be read the third time and passed.

subtopic: REGULATION OF PRODUCTS USED IN CONTROL PROCEDURE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am not going to be too long in debating this bill which was gone into at length in committee, but there are one or two matters that I believe should once again be raised, not for the advice of Your Honour, not necessarily for the knowledge of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson), but specifically for the information of the members of this chamber and the people of Canada in general. It has been stated both in the press and on the radio that there is a growing fear that a police state is developing in this country. The minister shakes his head indicating a negative answer.

subtopic: REGULATION OF PRODUCTS USED IN CONTROL PROCEDURE
speechtext: Exactly the opposite.

subtopic: REGULATION OF PRODUCTS USED IN CONTROL PROCEDURE
speechtext:
The minister says from his seat "exactly the opposite". I am pleased to hear him make that comment, because this is the second piece of agricultural legislation that has granted huge powers to an individual of the minister's choosing. Under clause 6 of this bill, the minister may designate any qualified person to be an inspector under the act.
An inspector under this act is given license to open the door and enter any premises. An ordinary policeman must have a search warrant to enter a house to see whether or not drugs, for example, are on the premises; but an inspector under this act can walk into any premises without notice and carry out an inspection in any way he wishes.
Although the minister says that we are moving in the opposite direction, I have already told the house that this is the second piece of legislation connected with agriculture that grants huge powers to an individual of

March 7, 1969
Control of Pesticide Use the minister's choosing. Other pieces of legislation similar to this are continually being brought before the house to grant wide powers to individuals who, in a policeman-like manner are permitted to control use of products, or the marketing or manufacture of such products.
Therefore, I must caution the country at this time, through you, Mr. Speaker, that unless we are prepared to honour these civil liberties that we often speak of in this chamber, some day we may find ourselves severely restrained and policed. This would mean that new ideas and products, or new uses of existing products, would be restricted.
That is the point I wanted to raise on third reading of this bill, particularly so far as clauses 6 and 7 are concerned. Clause 6 gives the minister the power to choose inspectors, and clause 7 outlines the duties of such inspectors. According to this bill, inspectors may enter any place or premises for the purpose of carrying out the provisions of the act.
As a result of this provision, wide powers are conferred. The acts deals with many situations and products, including pesticides which, in a sense, are lethal drugs. Inspectors are given the power to control the normal and beneficial use of drugs and insecticides. These inspectors are given more power than we give our own police to control the spread of drugs in society.
As I say, this is the second piece of agricultural legislation that has conferred such powers, and we have seen similar powers conferred in other legislation since this government has taken office. I, therefore, raise that warning and hope it will be heard, particularly by the backbenchers of the Liberal party. I trust that this trend, or what appears to be a trend, into which the country is drifting will be stopped.

subtopic: REGULATION OF PRODUCTS USED IN CONTROL PROCEDURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a few observations to make with regard to this bill. We have dealt with other bills in similar form that control people's actions, shall we say, because we are living in this modem age of technology. When we take this step, I think the law should have some special application to this end. My main complaint against this particular bill is that it contains provisions to enable individuals who fall afoul of the regulations made pursuant to the act to be prosecuted.
I do not think we should adopt the standard criminal procedures and apply them to actions that are taken under regulations of 
this kind. I cannot see any need for a provision in this bill to enable an individual who has violated the terms of the act to be indicted and made liable to imprisonment for two years. I do not think this situation should be permitted. The emphasis and the provision should be civil, and if I misuse the term I am sorry, but the approach should be the imposition of a fine. If a retailer or someone who operates a factory persists in violating the act, some move could be made against his operation for a period of time. An individual who has violated this act should not be classed as a criminal. It is outdated for an inspector to go to a justice of the peace, who may or may not be knowledgeable in the law, in respect of someone who in his opinion has violated this act. The inspector should go to a proper magistrate. I would assume that if there were a miscarriage of justice in this initial stage and the individual were charged, there would be a right of appeal. However, this litigation will cost him time and money.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
Legislation of this type should not put the individual to any more trouble or inconvenience than is necessary to control dangerous pesticides. These can be very dangerous if used in the wrong time and place by people not aware of the possible consequences. People who act in this manner are not necessarily criminals. This is what concerns me, Mr. Speaker. The individual must not bear any more burden than is absolutely necessary. These measures may not appear important to urban dwellers.
There are five counties in the province of Ontario which have regulations concerning the movement of farm material, and these affect many farmers. I do not expect the government will change this bill at the third reading stage, but I would urge them in future to tailor the provisions of the law so that they will specifically achieve the objective which is desired.

subtopic: REGULATION OF PRODUCTS USED IN CONTROL PROCEDURE
speechtext:
This bill, Mr. Speaker, seeks to control quality and distribution of pest control products. It can be deemed an honourable objective to improve the quality and method of production of these products which, as a result of experience, have shown deleterious effects when improperly manufactured or applied. Beyond that this bill is the most bureaucratic nonsense I have yet come across.
March 7, 1969

I spoke on Bills C-154, C-156 and now C-157. The minister has come up with a scissors and paste job on various sections of acts completely wiping out the rights of the individual vis-a-vis the bureaucracy that would enforce this act. I know this is quite immaterial to the minister who likes to let the juggernaut of the big government employee or representative roll over the rights of the individual.
Regulations can be made under this act, none of which require to be published. When speaking recently on one of the other acts the minister protested and said they will be published, but there is no guarantee that any regulation must be published. There is still provision in the Regulations Act that the Governor in Council can deem it necessary or expedient that the regulations shall not be published.

subtopic: REGULATION OF PRODUCTS USED IN CONTROL PROCEDURE
speechtext: But we will publish them, as I told you.

subtopic: REGULATION OF PRODUCTS USED IN CONTROL PROCEDURE
speechtext:
As I said the other day, Mr. Speaker, the road to Hades is paved with good intentions. These are only pious intentions. The minister's statements are not worth one iota in determining legal rights in the interpretation of this act. When it comes to a court of law, if one is able to do so, the minister's words or those of anyone else are meaningless. I ask the minister to get advice from the judicial offices of the Crown as to what is binding upon a court. We are interested in the precise letter of the law, nothing more, nothing less, rather than the minister's interpretations. The court must reach its own conclusions.
I now turn to the question of detention of products. It is the inspector who determines the seizure and detention of products. He decides how long they are to be detained or if they are to be destroyed at the owner's expense. He ensures that the provisions of the act and the regulations have been complied with, "or at the expiration of six months from the day of seizure, or such longer period as may be prescribed with respect to any control product"-
There is no statutory guarantee as to the length of time products may be detained. My colleague, the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner) mentioned the powers of an inspector under Clause 7. As I indicated when speaking on the other bills, any qualified person acting as an inspector for the purposes of this act can move into any premises at a reasonable time. What is a reasonable time? Is it any 29180-4031
Control oj Pesticide Use time between six in the morning and ten at night or even midnight? The inspector may examine any product, search the premises and may require the production of books and bills.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
There is no appeal from this provision. The man is given a certificate indentifying him as an inspector of the Minister of Agriculture for the purposes of this statute. Then he has complete right to do what he sees fit within the ambit of the regulations set by the minister. As I pointed out, police officials in search of drugs or of stolen property must have search warrants, but there is no necessity for a search warrant under this legislation.
This is bureaucracy run rampant, yet members on the government side of the house sit silent. They are the ones who are making a great show about a just society and the protection of individual liberties. It is hypocrisy on their part for them to remain silent in this case.
It is not so much the agricultural aspect of this bill that bothers me as it is the question of legal rights. Hon. members opposite laugh. I hope some day they will laugh on the other side of their faces. I hope some of them will run into circumstances where one of their constituents is caught by this provision. Then, we will see them bleating to the minister that one of their constituents has been ill treated. If that happens it will be because they have allowed the minister to ride rough shod over the rights of the individual by allowing this provision to remain in the bill.
Let us look again at clause 9, dealing with seizure and detention, and with the regulations to be made under this clause. As I said we have taken scissors and paste, taken provisions from the acts and put them altogether in this statute embracing all these offences.
The other day in committee we were dealing with Bill S-4 concerning the marking of articles made of precious metals. I argued with respect to a clause dealing with offences that the word "knowingly" had to be inserted. The minister agreed to consult the law officers of the Crown and later the government itself brought forward an amendment to insert the word. Precisely the same clause is in this bill as originally was in bill S-4.

March 7, 1969
Control of Pesticide Use
I shall read clause 10 which states:
Every person who, or whose employee or agent, violates any provision of this act or the regulations is guilty of
(a)	an indictable offence and is liable to imprisonment for two years, or
(b)	an offence punishable on summary conviction.
In other words, a person does not even have to know he has violated the provisions of the act to be subject to a penalty of up to two years imprisonment for an indictable offence. The minister's colleague says that an offence must be committed knowingly, but the Department of Agriculture says a person is absolutely liable. Do we accept that? Is that the proper standard for justice?

subtopic: REGULATION OF PRODUCTS USED IN CONTROL PROCEDURE
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member one question?

subtopic: REGULATION OF PRODUCTS USED IN CONTROL PROCEDURE
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: REGULATION OF PRODUCTS USED IN CONTROL PROCEDURE
speechtext: The person is dealing with lethal products. Shouldn't he know what he is doing?

subtopic: REGULATION OF PRODUCTS USED IN CONTROL PROCEDURE
speechtext: But there are so many ways of violating any provision in this statute, and of violating regulations that are not even published.

subtopic: REGULATION OF PRODUCTS USED IN CONTROL PROCEDURE
speechtext: They will be.

subtopic: REGULATION OF PRODUCTS USED IN CONTROL PROCEDURE
speechtext:
The minister says they will be. He is talking hot air, and he knows it, when he says they will necessarily be published. There is another point that the minister has failed to mention, that the burden of proof under this statute is placed upon the person himself. Clause 10(2) reads:
In any prosecution for an offence under this act, it is sufficient proof of the offence to establish that it was committed by an employee or agent of the accused whether or not the employee or agent is identified or has been prosecuted for the offence, unless the accused establishes that the offence was committed without his knowledge or consent and that he exercised all due diligence to prevent its commission.
The burden of proof is on the accused to show that he did not know his employee was doing something in strict contravention of the act.
The minister says that these are dangerous products. I ask what about narcotics? Yet the minister arms his inspectors with far greater powers than the police have when dealing with narcotic cases.
I agree there has to be some control over pest control products, but do we need this type of control when the minister proposes to

trample over the rights of individuals in every possible way merely to satisfy a bureaucratic desire to have simple administration? It can be the rights of an individual, of a manufacturer, of a large corporation or of a small corporation. It does not matter which because this legislation will ride rough shod over their rights.
The minister has the support of hon. members sitting behind him who say nothing. As I said previously, I hope to goodness that one of these days they will laugh on the other side of their faces when one of their constituents comes to them because of action taken by the minister's officials under this legislation. I dare say most of the hon. members opposite have not read clause 5 outlining the powers given to the Governor in Council to make regulations. As so aptly pointed out by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin), they are prohibited from raising these points in committee.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
An hon. member opposite laughs. I would just like to tell him that when we were dealing with Bill S-4 in the standing committee and I was arguing that the word "knowingly" had to be inserted in order for a person to commit an offence, Liberal members of the committee, lawyers included, started to argue that I was all wrong and that it was not necessary to insert the word. However, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Basford) had the good sense not to argue the case then, and simply said he would consult with the law officers of the Crown. It took him only 24 hours to let me know that he thought I was right on that point. Under the powers given to the Governor in Council by clause 5, regulations can be made that will tie up anyone and deliver him impotent for trial as the bureaucracy wishes. We are quite supine in this house when we give the cabinet all this power. We wash our hands of the thing like Pilate; that is what we think of the rights of individual citizens when we pass bills of this kind. I for one will vote against this bill not because I disagree with the fact of pest control but because I disagree with the method proposed by the government in doing this.

subtopic: REGULATION OF PRODUCTS USED IN CONTROL PROCEDURE
speechtext:
I, too, Mr. Speaker, am very concerned about this legislation. Under clause 7 of this bill powers are granted to an inspector who is not the choice of a group of people and who has not been elected. The inspector is to be appointed by
March 7, 1969

one man and is to be given far more power than are the police or any other official body in this nation. In all other fields of law, we are very concerned about civil rights. Even murderers, thieves and extortionists are given rights. Sometimes they are given rights that make conviction seem impossible. Yet, here we are putting into effect regulations which virtually make farmers the slaves of bureaucratic whim and which make private property rights in the agricultural segment virtually non-existent. Farmers have no guarantee of their rights in this regard. We all know that when laws are made they seldom are retracted. In the aggregate, we end up in a morass of regulations and controls which stifle personal initiative.
As my colleague the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) has stated already the burden of proof in areas relating to ordinary crime is such that the individual is considered to be innocent until proven guilty. Are the farmers of this nation such terrible citizens that they must be guilty until they can prove themselves innocent? The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) has always seemed to me to be a reasonable man and therefore I ask him, for heaven's sake, and for the sake of the people in agriculture to please reconsider this clause.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to rise on a question of privilege, and I beg your indulgence in permitting me to elaborate in some detail. Everybody in the house is aware of the controversy which surrounds the Canadian seal fishing industry and also that earlier in the week the minister announced his intention to visit the Atlantic area and the Gulf of St. Lawrence to personally view this operation. I think most hon. members are aware that I was personally invited to go on this trip by our caucus chairman, the hon. member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse), as a member of the fisheries committee.
As a result, the radio, television and newspaper media, were notified that this visit was to be made. From the comments received it was apparent that many Canadians were happy there would be somebody present who understood something about the other side of the story.
This trip was scheduled for 2.30 p.m. today. Despite very stringent commitments on my part and on the part of other members of our party in respect of party work, we were ready and arrangements were made so that I could personally make the visit. I was informed this morning at 9.30 that the time of departure was advanced to one o'clock, or an hour and a half earlier, the excuse being that weather conditions would not be suitable for tomorrow's activities.
I accepted this fact and, after, a great deal of confusion amongst members, it was conveniently arranged that I make the trip at one o'clock or a few minutes after in order that I might be with the minister and other members of the committee on this visit to the Atlantic region. I hope these remarks will not indicate any childishness on my part in not being able to attend, but I can only draw the conclusion that this was an attempt to prevent any representative of the people who had any
March 7, 1969	COMMONS
knowledge of these fisheries problems from taking part in the visit.
My question of privilege is that when public facilities are being used for this purpose an opportunity should be given for representation of a cross-section of the Canadian public. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on this bill, another piece of legislation dealing with farm credit, which is a subject of concern to the whole agricultural industry today. I very much wonder whether this bill will meet the purposes that it was once designed to meet. I remember about three years ago the former minister of agriculture, who is now in the other place, outlined his hopes and aspirations for this piece of legislation. At that time he said this measure would cure all the ills with which farmers were confronted. He said it would allow them to buy machinery jointly, which would lower their costs of production and thereby reduce the cost-price squeeze. About that time, the minister paid a glowing tribute to the legislation at a meeting in Lethbridge with the farmers of Alberta. This was about three years ago.
The legislation was presented to parliament and debated at length in this House of Commons. I said at that time that the legislation would have to do more, it would have to go further, if it were to be applicable to farming conditions and in any way fulfil a small portion of the minister's hopes and aspirations.
It does me some good to see some of the suggestions for which I argued three years ago now included in the bill. At that time farm machinery was covered. I said this was not good enough; the bill should also cover the purchase of land on which buildings could be placed. I said at that time that a building could very well be a component part of a machine or could in a sense be the entire machine. At that time I gave a lengthy definition of what was an agricultural implement and what was an agricultural machine. I asked: Did it have to have moving parts, or not? In any case, Mr. Speaker, I could not at that time convince the minister, after lengthy debate. I am sure the minister recalls the debate.

I argued for the inclusion of buildings and land on which buildings could be placed, but they were not included in the bill. I also argued for two or three other things that should be included in the bill. I should like to bring to the attention of the house those things which I argued should be included in the bill about three years ago, because perhaps three years from now the same minister or a different one will recognize that the application of the act is not nearly as broad as he thought it might be and will look for ways in which it can have broader application.
I say this, Mr. Speaker, because this act has not had very broad application. It has in fact, been very restricted in its application. It has application to family corporations or groups of farmers, sons, daughters, cousins or uncles, who are farming and can conceivably use a machine if they join forces. They can then borrow money under the act. This is the purpose for which the act has primarily been used. I do not hesitate to say that something like 66 per cent of the loans made under the act to date have been made to what one might call family clans comprising of perhaps uncles, sons, daughters, and so on, farming separately. They have banded together to buy machinery under the act.

speechtext: You mean family farmers.

speechtext:
I mean families farming
entirely for themselves, but the relationship existing for a family farm. The minister is mumbling away to himself, but he does not deny the 66 per cent figure which I mentioned. I think this is very close to being the fact. But if you accept that figure, you must ask yourselves why the application of the act has been narrowed and confined to groups of farmers related by blood, brothers-in-law, uncles, sisters, or what have you.
The minister has done this for one reason. That reason can only be that loans under the act must be jointly and severally held. In other words, the act provides that a maximum amount of $100,000 may be borrowed if seven farmers participate. The act suggests that they do not all have to be farmers, but the majority of them have to be farmers. The old act suggested that they all had to be farmers.
However, Mr. Speaker, that is not the point I am now trying to make. The point is that each person can borrow $15,000, and that is all he can borrow. But seven or more farmers can borrow up to a maximum of $100,000. In
March 7, 1969

this event, each person who joins the syndicate has to sign a promissory note making himself liable for $100,000. In other words, while his credit is good for only $15,000 as one-seventh of the syndicate, he has to sign a promissory note accepting liability for the total amount of $100,000. So instead of the government getting security for the $100,000, if there are seven people in the syndicate the government gets security for $700,000. Aren't they big, brave, bold lenders? I cannot accept that they are. What is the situation here? A member joining a syndicate, signing up for $100,000 and receiving the benefit of only $15,000 does so only on those occasions when he benefits the clan generally. I use the word "clan" quite generally.
When this bill was first introduced in the house about three years ago I said this was the wrong principle. I said that if the government wanted a wide application of the bill it should allow a person to sign a promissory note for that portion of the money which he was prepared to accept from the syndicate, whether it be one-fifth, one-seventh or one-hundredth. He should have to sign a promissory note for that portion only.
The minister, and the chairman of the Farm Credit Corporation, a man who I know is doing his best to have the act applied in a wide manner, have continually told me that all this is not really necessary, that the real security under the act is the machine itself for which the syndicate borrowed money. Although the machine might deteriorate, they can always pick it up. If there is a default in any way, the machine can always be picked up. Then, the government would have the machine, and I suppose in that case the syndicate would go broke or would in any event forfeit its use of the machine.
We were told that there was really nothing to worry about; farmers could just sign a promissory note for $100,000, and there would never be a foreclosure because the machine itself was part of the security. This is all the more reason for the government accepting the fact that a promissory note held jointly and severally under this act is not necessary. In fact, any wise, prudent financial operator would not sign a note for $100,000. It just is not good business sense to sign a note for $100,000 and receive the benefit of only $15,000. If the minister wants a wide application of this act, I urge him to consider this point.
When the bill was studied in committee it was pointed out that there was one syndicate that had 87 members. Under the bill the 87

When you have 87 members in a syndicate, you can bet your bottom dollar that even if five or six of them go broke and are unable to meet their liability in respect of the promissory notes, 81 or 82 members will still pick up the tab.

But if you have only seven in a syndicate, and three of them found all of a sudden they had to pay income tax on a lot of money, had to sell their holdings to do so and they did not have much security, you would be left with four people to pick up the $100,000. Then, the trouble would begin. Stringent measures may have to be taken in the years ahead in view of the present government's attitude toward collecting money. However, this is another subject with which I should like to deal at some other time. I do not believe the provisions under this act will be of great use to farmers if the government repeatedly insists that loans must be jointly and severally held. There is no reason for it. If the government really believes that the agricultural industry needs financial assistance and that loans should be made for farm machinery, it is the government's duty to make that money available to everybody, whether or not they are members of a large clan and can make use of it because of the security of the clan.
The minister must be well aware of the fact, because I have repeated it in the house several times, that the Economic Council of Canada stated in its report last fall that the agricultural industry in this country was in severe need of financing and that it was 20 years behind the agricultural industry in the United States. Surely after having read this pointed recommendation on the one way in which our industry can catch up and compete with the United States industry, the minister should make every effort to have this act apply in the widest possible way. He should make it available on an equal basis to every farmer in Canada, not just a few members of a clan or family who are farming close together and who can avail themselves of the security of the family to obtain money advanced under this act.
I would like the minister to study the question seriously. If 66 per cent of the loans under this act are in fact made to family clans, then there is a reason for it. The minister should consider this fact seriously. If

The second point I want to make concerns the Farm Machinery Syndicates Credit Act and farm implements. In the act we see that additional land and buildings have been added. I ask the minister: Why not cattle? Surely, in this highly technological age we have reached a sufficient degree of refinement of definitions in the field of agriculture to realize that cattle are machines which change crude proteins to refined and digestible proteins. This is, in effect, what they do. We have heard that the former minister of agriculture who is now a member of the other place came up with a new breed of cattle which he called the Hays' converter. I agree with my colleague, the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin), that it would be pretty rough beef, and I would hate to eat it.
I see the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) is back in his seat and I should like to deal with his attitude to the problem. The Hays' converter is an example I gave to prove to the minister that he and his department should give serious consideration to adding to clause 3 paragraph (d) "to purchase feeder cattle". I am not referring to the purchase of grass cattle but rather to the final stage of the livestock industry. I am not saying we should get into the cow-calf operation and raise livestock. I am referring to the final stage of the industry which would consist of buying feeder cattle and converting them to digestible proteins and beef.
If the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce had ventured into western Canada lately and watched some of the cattle sales that took place last month and this month, he would realize that this converter factor is related to the fact the cattle are being fed grain. Let him try and buy some of these cattle. Who is buying them? Farmers with surplus grain and damp grain which the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce has not sold. Why are they paying such high


prices for them? Because they want to convert the damp grain, wheat and feed grains from an unsaleable product, from a crude protein, to a digestible protein. They are using the cattle as machines or as converters, as the minister suggests. I say that in the past ten years it has never been proven, in the highly technological age to which we have advanced that cattle are in fact machines. I am sure that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) knows very well what I am speaking about when I refer to conversion. If he wants me to go further into the subject as to whether or not they are machines, let us look at what is ahead.
Animals are now being developed in test tubes in laboratories so that the whole gestation period in the animal's body may become unnecessary. Experiments of this kind are being carried out in scientific laboratories all over the world. Whether we like it or not, this may well happen in the future.
While I do not want to belabour the point, I hope the minister will seriously consider whether the farm machinery syndicates credit legislation can be made applicable on as wide a basis as possible. I know the minister can say there are other ways of providing money to the cattle and livestock industry, and that money can be borrowed under the farm improvement loans legislation. That is the weakest argument I have ever heard, because the Minister of Agriculture knows and the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce should know how many cattle it takes to move a thousand bushels of grain and what kind of machinery it takes to move that amount of grain. The initial, capital cost of that machine is not the cheapest thing in the world.
Under the farm improvement loans legislation around $15,000 can be borrowed for the purchase of feeder cattle. This is hardly enough. I believe that if this legislation made $100,000 available it would do some good. The minister says the opposition never offers constructive suggestions. Well, I have put forward two extremely important constructive suggestions as to ways in which this act could be improved and I should like him to give them serious consideration.

subtopic: TRANSCOASTAL LIFE INSURANCE COMPANY
TRANSCOASTAL LIFE INSURANCE COMPANY
speechtext:
the second reading and reference to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs of Bill S-16, to incorporate Transcoastal Life Insurance Company.

March 7, 1969
Private Bills
He said: The purpose of this bill is to incorporate a Canadian life insurance company to take over the existing business in Canada of the Union Mutual Life Insurance Company of Portland, Maine. This company has carried on business in Canada since 1868. In recent years its Canadian business has grown very extensively and it is a corporate decision of the directors and officers of the company that, having regard to the growth of its business, Canadian residents who now hold its policies would be better served by a company domiciled in Canada and governed by a board of directors the majority of whom would be Canadian citizens.
This bill is in the form of a model bill prescribed in the insurance company legislation with one important addition. There is included in it a provision similar to that which was included in a bill enacted by this parliament in 1967 providing for the orderly transfer of ownership in this country from United States owners to Canadian citizens. This clause provides that in the first five years after incorporation at least 25 per cent of the shares of the stock of the company would be made available to Canadian residents and that in the succeeding five years another 24 per cent would be made available, and if the general legislation made it easy I am informed that the company would willingly provide for the transfer of majority control.
It has been the custom in this chamber to provide merely a general introduction to such legislation as this on second reading, it being well understood that when the bill is referred to committee the members of that committee will have an opportunity to examine the officers and promoters of the legislation in detail.

subtopic: TRANSCOASTAL LIFE INSURANCE COMPANY
speechtext:
The sponsor of the bill has indicated that this is an application by a United States corporation to Incorporate a Canadian insurance company. As he pointed out, the principal shareholder will be the Union Mutual Company which has operated a branch office in Canada for the last hundred years.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
The most significant breakthrough is clause 8 of the bill which, as the sponsor said, will give an opportunity for Canadians in the first five years of the incorporation to acquire a 25 per cent interest and within a ten year period a 49 per cent interest. He also indicated that it may be the desire of the company to have a majority Canadian interest in the future.

This is a real breakthrough with regard to the problem of foreign ownership in Canada. As the house knows, many members of our party, particularly the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) and the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters), have led a campaign in regard to insurance companies and loan and trust companies the purpose of which was to make sure that there is a Canadian content in such companies. Thus far they had succeeded only with one company. We now have a second company that incorporates in its bill the provision to provide for Canadian ownership.
We would like to congratulate the sponsor of the bill on the acceptance of this principle. Looking across and seeing the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) recalls to my mind the opinions he expressed on the problem of economic nationalism and continentalism. I think he summed them up during a debate on estimates in this way, continentalism if necessary but not necessarily continentalism.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: TRANSCOASTAL LIFE INSURANCE COMPANY
speechtext: May I correct that. I said that I could be a continentalist if it were in the national interest.

subtopic: TRANSCOASTAL LIFE INSURANCE COMPANY
speechtext:
I am prepared to accept the minister's interpretation. Since he is a most fair and generous minister I should not like to place an interpretation upon his statement that he would think unfair. This underlines the fact that the voice in the wilderness of the past in point of time becomes the accepted opinion of most Canadians. We in the New Democratic party are rather proud that we have advanced the proposition that where there is United States participation in the Canadian economy it should be on a partnership basis, and that Canadian shareholders should be given the opportunity to participate in the activities and ownership of such companies.
I am going to read portions of a letter that was sent to me and to other members of my party regarding the attitude of this particular company. The letter was sent by the vicepresident and counsel for the applicant, a gentleman named Douglas Thornsjo, and reads:
You may recall that our sincere feeling is that all of our Canadian business belongs in a Canadian company, with a Canadian board of directors, and within a reasonable time with widespread Canadian ownership. It is our further feeling that, not only is this the fair or equitable manner by which to do business in Canada, but that in the long run, we will do better with one half or even less
March 7, 1989

of a Canadian company than we would be able to do as a United States company.
In return, what does the Canadian nation receive through this process? We believe the "bargain" clearly favours Canada because:
1)	it establishes the precedent that U.S. citizens are willing to do business in Canada as partners with Canadians and not as financial owners of Canada:
2)	it causes an existing U.S. company to withdraw from Canada because, at the end of the first calendar year of Transcoastal's licensed existence, Union Mutual by agreement will withdraw from doing any new business in Canada. In addition, all existing Union Mutual, Canadian business will be serviced (premiums paid through, questions answered by, beneficiary changes effected by, and claims paid by) the new Canadian company;
3)	investment dollars now flowing to the United States will be retained in Canada. Indeed, if the Canadian company were entered into the United States, a current probability, U.S. dollars would flow into Canada;
4)	Canadian payroll will be substantially increased;
5)	the Transcoastal bill helps to establish a precedent of safeguards pertinent to any effort which the government might take to present a bill removing from parliament the burden of handling private member, business oriented bills. In other words, some sentiment exists to the effect that private member bills such as S-16 should not take the time of parliament. The government might well be sympathetic to such sentiment. But
Private Bills
it should be made clear, in advance, that any generalized authority to charter companies outside of parliament must contain safeguards for the concept of Canadian ownership. No better technique exists than that of precedent; the precedent of failure of private bills without provision for Canadian ownership and the corelevant precedent of success for at least an occasional bill that does provide for Canadian ownership.
The vice-president set forth our views regarding this very serious problem. We are proud to permit the bill to pass and to be sent to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs for further study.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.
